questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I always wanted to experience Canada, and Vancouver seemed like an interesting city close to nature. Furthermore, as a MSc student it was a lot easier to go to UBC than many of the other North American universities.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I had already gotten most of the information I needed from the UBC Go Global website and from previous online orientations, so I didn't need much more information upon arrival. However, it seemed very clear who to ask for assistance if needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an orientation on the first day (Imagine Day). It was pretty boring, as I had already heard most of the information beforehand. There was a small tour of the campus and some social acitivities, which was nice enough.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: My boyfriend and I lived together in Vancouver, we found accommodation via a Facebook group (Danes in Vancouver). We ended up renting a suite in the house of a Danish family and were happy with that. It went smoothly and the rent was very reasonable, but it was quite far from the university. We also considered renting via Airbnb - it would have been more expensive, so in that case, we would probably have tried to find a few other students to share a place with. Vancouver is a really expensive city to live in, so sharing a place is a good option for off-campus housing.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: UBC is far away from downtown! If you want to have a social life there, definitely try to find accomodation in West Point Grey, Dunbar, or Kitsilano. However, if you are more interested in exploring the city and the wonderful nature of the North Shore, it is easier if you live closer to downtown. I lived in West Vancouver, which I think most people would think is way too far away from UBC and too quiet, but it is a nice neighbourhood and a short drive from the mountains. If you are more into nightlife (which is not a big thing in Vancouver), quirky shops, cozy cafés etc., East Vancouver is really cool but also far from university. Avoid the Downtown Eastside, that's where the homeless people live, and unfortunately there are a lot of problems with drug abuse and homelessness.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think around 50% of the exchange students got housing on campus.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: First, I had to fill out the top 10 courses that I wanted (although I only needed to register for 3 as a MSc student). It was quite difficult because they were supposed to overlap as little as possible, and I could only fill in undergraduate courses (i.e. 100-400 level courses) and courses with no restrictions, as graduate courses are applied for through a different (and much more tedious) process. I got registered in some of the top courses, but in one instance the tutorial section was missing, and I had to register for it manually although I was supposedly not allowed to. For the 500-level course I took, I had to fill out a form and send it to the instructors, then to the section head and then to the department of graduate studies. The process was very slow, so I was still not registered at the beginning of the semester, but thankfully you are allowed to switch courses during the first few weeks of the semester. I also tried to enroll in another grad course, but it turned out that it was not really a course but more of a weekly discussion meeting, so that didn't work out.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I got some help from Go Global, but they could not do much except telling me to be patient and advising me to attend the course I was not registered in until the registration came through.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In the end, I was happy about my courses, although it took a bit of time and worries. One course was registrated through the form (but not the tutorial section, which I had to do myself), one course I registered for via the grad-course form, and one restricted course I registered for by writing to the course responsible. I had hoped to get more grad-level courses, but it was okay.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to find lots of courses that you are interested in attending, so that you have alternatives if you don't get your top priorities. Don't be afraid to try and register in restricted courses, just try and reach out to the course responsible. Ask Go Global for advice if in doubt.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Two of my courses were 400-level (but one of them was mostly attended by grad students) and one of them was 500-level. If you are a MSc student, be aware that many 400-level courses are attended by both undergrad and graduate students and can usually be approved as MSc-level courses. On the other hand, be aware that UBC has both thesis and non-thesis graduate programmes, and in some cases the courses aimed at on-thesis students may not be as academic as you are used to from UCPH (e.g. less focus on primary literature).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was quite similar, but more focused on tests and assignments.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
FOOD 521 Advances in food biotechnology
FRST 475 Indigenous ecologies
MICB 405 Bioinformatics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
MICB 405 was a very nice bioinformatics course, the teachers are great, and you get a good overview of different methods, applications etc. There is also a team project.
I also thought that FRST 475 was extremely interesting and very different from other courses I have attended. However, the workload was surprisingly high. 
FOOD 521 was nice enough and had some labs and seminars, but the students came from many different backgrounds, and a lot of the lectures were repetition of basic molecular biology.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Greens and veggies are much more expensive than in Denmark. However, you can get cheaper meals at restaurants, and things like beer and coffee are generally cheap, too.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a ton of clubs, which are introduced on the very first day of the semester. There are also great options for sports and exercise.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I mostly made use of the free access to the aquatic centre. If you like swimming, it is a great option!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore the neighbourhoods of Vancouver - especially East Vancouver (e.g. Commercial Drive, Main Street), West End and Stanley Park. Taste the local craft beer varieties and explore the vintage shops etc. Go hiking and skiing in the local mountains and Whistler. Visit Vancouver Island (especially Tofino), but make sure you have enough time to get around - it is not a huge island, but it takes a long time to get there and to drive around.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Vancouverites are not very outgoing, so I found it a little challenging to get close to the local students. Also, many of the students I met were from India and China, and some of them did not speak very good English, which made communication a bit difficult.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I liked how polite everybody are - e.g. saying 'thank you' when leaving the bus. I really like that Vancouver is such a multicultural place, it is great to see people from all over the world living happily together.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Know your priorities - if you want 'campus life', you need to live there or at least quite close. UBC is far from downtown, and the buses make getting around very slow. You can bike, but campus is uphill from downtown...
2) Be aware that you will probably have to hand in a lot more assignments, quizzes etc. than you may be used to. Plan any extended weekend trips accordingly.
3) Canada is huge, so don't expect to see a lot of it during your exchange. If you have the time and money, consider travelling around before or after your stay to see a bit more than just Vancouver and its surroundings.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing a different culture, getting some new perspective on Danish culture and my own place in the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Socializing with the local students, especially because I was a grad student and living far from campus (however, I knew beforehand that this would probably make it more difficult to be part of campus life - pros and cons)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you are keen on going skiing, consider going in the spring - there is no guarantee of cold weather in December.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
